concepts.label: Motion in a Straight Line and Describing Position
concepts.cardText: When an object moves in a straight line its motion is called linear motion, the simplest kind of motion. To describe the position of an object we first specify a fixed point as the reference point. The distance and direction of the object from the reference point at any instant describe its position at that instant. For an object moving in a straight line there are only two directions, forward and backward, represented by plus and minus signs, with positions to the right of the reference point O generally taken as positive and to the left as negative. If the position of the object with respect to the reference point changes with time, the object is in motion; if it does not change with time, the object is at rest.

concepts.label: Distance Travelled and Displacement
concepts.cardText: The total distance travelled by an athlete who runs from O to A (100 m) and back to B (60 m) is OA + AB = 160 m, but the distance between the starting and stopping positions is OB = 40 m. Displacement is the net change in the position of an object between two given instants of time. A complete description of displacement requires specifying both a direction and its numerical value with units, called its magnitude. The magnitude of displacement is the distance between the object's positions at the two instants, and its direction is from the position at the first instant towards the position at the second instant. To describe total distance travelled only the numerical value is needed, not the direction, and the SI unit for both is the metre. In the example the athlete's total distance travelled is 160 m but her displacement is 40 m in the positive direction. For motion in a straight line the total distance travelled and the magnitude of displacement are equal if the object moves without turning back, in one direction.

concepts.label: Average Speed and Uniform Motion
concepts.cardText: The average speed of an object is the total distance travelled divided by the time interval during which this distance is covered. Since distance travelled has no direction, the average speed also has no direction but only a numerical value. If an object moving in a straight line travels equal distances in equal intervals of time, for all possible choices of time intervals, it is in uniform motion in a straight line and moves at a constant speed. If it travels unequal distances in equal intervals of time it is in non-uniform motion, moving with increasing speed, decreasing speed, or a combination of both. The speed tells how fast an object moves but gives no information about the direction of motion. The idea of speed as distance travelled divided by time taken dates back to ancient times in India, as in the Aryabhatiya.

concepts.label: Average Velocity and Rate of Change
concepts.cardText: The average velocity of an object in a time interval is the change in position, or displacement, divided by the time interval in which the change occurs. To express average velocity we specify its magnitude as well as direction, and the direction of velocity is the same as the direction of displacement, indicated by a plus or minus sign. The SI unit of average speed and average velocity is metre per second, also commonly measured in kilometre per hour. The ratio of change in one quantity to the corresponding change in time is called the rate of change, so average velocity is the average rate of change of position with respect to time. In Example 4.2, Sarang swims 50 m in 50 s, up and back, so his total distance is 50 m, displacement is 0 m, average speed is about 1 m per second and average velocity is 0. For motion in a straight line the average speed and the magnitude of average velocity are equal if the object moves in one direction. The average velocity over a large interval may differ from the velocity at a particular instant.

concepts.label: Average Acceleration
concepts.cardText: The average acceleration of an object over a time interval is the change in its velocity divided by the time interval. Like displacement and velocity, acceleration has both magnitude and direction. For motion in a straight line, if the magnitude of velocity is increasing the average acceleration is in the direction of velocity, whereas it is opposite to the direction of velocity if the magnitude of velocity is decreasing, shown by a minus sign. Acceleration can result from a change in the magnitude of velocity, a change in its direction, or both. An object can be moving very fast and yet have zero acceleration, because acceleration depends not on how fast an object is moving but on how quickly its velocity is changing. If the magnitude of velocity increases or decreases by equal amounts in equal intervals of time the acceleration is constant. A dropped object has a constant average acceleration of 9.8 metres per second squared in the direction of motion, called the acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g.

concepts.label: Position-Time Graphs
concepts.cardText: A position-time graph represents the change in position of an object with time; a graph is not a route map but shows how the position changes with time with respect to the origin. A straight-line position-time graph indicates that the object is moving with a constant velocity, whereas a curved graph indicates that the velocity is not constant and the object is in accelerated motion. The slope of a line is its steepness, and the slope of a graph gives the rate of change of the quantity on the Y-axis with respect to the quantity on the X-axis, so the slope of a position-time graph gives the average velocity. A straight line parallel to the time axis represents a stationary object. When two objects are compared, the one with the steeper line has the higher velocity.

concepts.label: Velocity-Time Graphs: Shape and Slope
concepts.cardText: A velocity-time graph represents the change in velocity of an object with time. When the velocity is constant the graph is a straight line parallel to the X-axis and the acceleration is zero. A straight-line velocity-time graph that rises indicates that the velocity is increasing with a constant acceleration in the direction of velocity, whereas a straight line that falls indicates that the velocity is decreasing with a constant acceleration opposite to the direction of velocity. The slope of the line on a velocity-time graph gives how fast the velocity is changing with time, that is the acceleration; a slope of zero means constant velocity and zero acceleration, and a minus sign means the acceleration is opposite to the velocity because the velocity is decreasing.

concepts.label: Velocity-Time Graphs: Area and Displacement
concepts.cardText: The area enclosed by a velocity-time graph and the time axis for a desired time interval is equal to the displacement in that time interval. For constant velocity the area of the rectangle is velocity times time interval, which equals the displacement, for example 120 m between 0 s and 6 s at 20 m per second. For motion with constant acceleration the area is a rectangle plus a triangle, so between 10 s and 20 s the displacement is the area of the rectangle plus the area of the triangle, 50 m plus 25 m, which is 75 m. By finding the slope and the area from the velocity-time graph for motion with constant acceleration we can determine acceleration and displacement, respectively.

concepts.label: Kinematic Equations for Constant Acceleration
concepts.cardText: For the special case of motion with constant acceleration, the acceleration at each instant equals the average acceleration over any time interval. From the definition of average acceleration the first equation is v = u + at, which lets us calculate the velocity at all times if the initial velocity and acceleration are known. The displacement s during time t is given by the area under the velocity-time graph, a rectangle plus a triangle, which gives the second equation. These two are the primary equations; combining them in different ways gives three more, of which one, v squared equals u squared plus 2as, is derived by eliminating t. For motion in a straight line with constant acceleration the five physical quantities displacement, time interval, initial velocity, final velocity and acceleration are related by these kinematic equations, which describe how the motion changes with time and let us predict position or velocity at a future time. They are valid only when the acceleration is constant, and in straight-line motion in both directions the signs of u, v, a and s tell their directions.

concepts.label: Braking Distance and Road Safety
concepts.cardText: In Example 4.8 a car brakes with an acceleration of -4 m per second squared. Starting from 54 km per hour the distance travelled before stopping is 28.1 m, and starting from 108 km per hour it is 112.5 m. When brakes are applied the vehicle moves some distance before stopping, and this distance depends upon the velocity of the vehicle when the brakes are applied, the road surface, the braking capacity of the vehicle, and the driver's reaction time. This is why it is important to maintain a safe distance from the vehicle ahead and adjust it according to your initial velocity. Vehicle-to-vehicle communication technology, being developed in many countries including India, lets vehicles exchange signals and warns drivers of possible collisions.

concepts.label: Uniform Circular Motion
concepts.cardText: Motion in a plane, such as a vehicle overtaking another, the path of a kicked ball or a satellite moving in a circular path, is called motion in two dimensions. When an object moves in a circular path its motion is called circular motion. For a child on a merry-go-round moving from A to B to C the distance travelled is the curve ABC and the displacement is the straight line AC, which are not equal; after one full revolution the distance is the circumference of the circle but the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero. When an object moves in a circular path with constant (uniform) speed, its motion is called uniform circular motion. As the number of sides of a track increases the track approaches a circle and the direction of the athlete's velocity changes continuously. A marble released from a ring moves in a straight line, continuing in the direction it was moving at that instant: the velocity at a point is along the tangent to the circle at that point. In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the motion is accelerated because the direction of velocity continuously changes. It is an idealised model, useful as a foundation for planets revolving around the Sun or a vehicle making a circular turn.
